Soulver on the Mac.



I recently stumbled on Literate Calc Mode by Robin1 that does everything I was using Soulver for, and I now have one more reason to not leave Emacs. It’s in Melpa, so installing it is simple. Once required, it provides both literate-calc-mode and literate-calc-minor-mode. I find the minor mode particularly useful for Org mode scratch buffers. For example, I used it recently to sketch out some details for a conference funding request. In an Org buffer, I entered:



Expenses for February 2027 Baylor Trip

Hotel = 500
Parking = 10
Registration = 295
Mileage = 300
Meals = 200

Total = Hotel + Parking + Registration + Mileage + Meals

M-x literate-calc-minor-mode instantly changed it to this:



Expenses for February 2027 Baylor Trip

Hotel = 500 => Hotel: 500
Parking = 10 => Parking: 10
Registration = 295 => Registration: 295
Mileage = 300 => Mileage: 300
Meals = 200 => Meals: 200

Total = Hotel + Parking + Registration + Mileage + Meals => Total: 1,305

=> is not editable and displayed in a lighter shade. Changing one of the variable values results in an instant update of the total. It uses Calc, so it is able to do almost anything that Calc can do. So far, I’ve used it to plan travel expenses and to build material lists for woodworking projects. It works flawlessly and I’ve found it surprisingly useful to have a scratchpad that can automatically do the math.

articles.description:
The ability to mark items in GNU Emacs Dired allows for bulk operations on both files and directories. With marking, onerous tasks can be turned into a trivial ones.
While default Dired has many bulk operation commands, not everything is covered. That is the motivation for mdired, an Elisp package which extends Dired with some SIMD-style commands.
Using these commands fall into two steps:
Mark the items of interest in Dired.
Run the mdired command.
mdired supports the following four commands:
mdired-copy: copy a single file to multiple directories.
mdired-do-command: run an Elisp command or named keyboard macro on multiple files.
mdired-compile: run compile on multiple directories.
mdired-byte-recompile: byte-compile selected files or directories.
Refer to the mdired User Guide for more details on usage.
Closing Thoughts
Bulk operation commands are chainsaws. Use them with caution. That said, they are great for improvised workflows:
“Here’s this file that I want copied to a bunch of directories.”
“I want to do the same edit operation on this set of files. I’ve got a named keyboard macro ready to go on them.”
“I want to run the same make command on a bunch of directories.”
As mdired is new, I’m open to feedback on it. Let me know what you think.
mdired v1.0 is now available on MELPA.

marking the active window (update here ) so that it’s easy to pick it out from the other, inactive windows. I did that by making the mode line of the active window a distinct color instead of the slightly different shade of gray from the other windows. That’s worked out really well for me and I’ve never looked back.


Now Ray Zeitler over at Ray on Emacs takes another look at the problem and found a really nice solution. It’s a bit more in your face than mine so if you’re looking for something that makes the active window really stand out, you should take a look at his post. The TL;DR is that instead of changing the active window, he changes the background color of all the other windows.


Zeitler found his solution on a 10 year old Stack Exchange post so it’s pretty certain to work no matter what version of Emacs you’re using. The code is very simple and you can simply copy it to your init.el if you’re interested.


As I said, this solution seems a little aggressive to me so I doubt I’ll be implementing it but others may disagree. One thing for sure, it’s going to make your active window stand out. It’s a small enough change that you can try it out—say by copying it to your scratch buffer and executing it—to see if it’s something you’d like.

The early history of Emacs involved the researchers at the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory agreeing on a standard set of TECO macros in order to improve collaboration. That was undoubtedly an ongoing process that didn’t have a well defined beginning or end so it’s easy to understand why the exact birthday of Emacs is a little murky.


Regardless, we can all celebrate Emacs’ 50th year. It’s remarkable when you think about it. Very few programs last that long. There’s FORTRAN and Lisp, of course, but I can’t think of any other piece of software with that sort of longevity. There is, to be sure, a Ship of Theseus aspect to that longevity but it’s one shared by FORTRAN and Lisp as well.


Who knows what things will look like in another 50 years but if we still have editors, I’m putting my money on Emacs still being around. Wouldn’t that be something?

Unicode punctuation in Emacs. His post is mainly concerned with the vagaries of dealing with English and Polish punctuation in the same document but a lot of the heavy lifting is accomplished with Electric Quote Mode.


The main problem is handling single and double quotes ‘like this’ and “like this”. Because I do almost all my writing in Org mode, I use the ':t option to turn the ASCII double quote (") into their curved typeset equivalents on export. That’s supposed to do the same with single quotes but I could never get it to work for me and always had to add then manually.


Fortunately, it’s easy to make everything work right in the buffer as you type. You merely turn electric-quote-mode on and it takes care of everything for you. By default it acts the way TeX used to by requiring “ for an opening double quote and ” for the closing double quote and similarly for single quotes. You can make it accept ” and ‘ instead by setting electric-quote-replace-double and electric-quote-context-sensitive to t.


Electric Quote Mode is global so turning it on enables it for all your buffers. You can use electric-quote-local-mode if you want it only in the current buffer. You can toggle either of them on or off by simply calling Meta+x electric-quote....


If you have to deal different quote notation for two or more languages, take a look at mbork’s post for a nifty solution.

new Emacs trick from Emacs Dwelling. Well, new to me. It turns out it’s been in Emacs since 28.1 so for about four and a half years.


Here’s the problem. When you call isearch it starts searching at the current point location to the bottom of the file. You can cause it to wrap around and continue searching at the top of the file but this isn’t always convenient. As a result, many people always start their search by moving to the top of the buffer first. But this isn’t always convenient either. For example, if you quit the search you go back to the top of the file, not where you started.


Sometimes you want a bit more control: perhaps you want to start at the first match or the last match and if you quit, you’d like to be back where you started. Well this is Emacs so of course you can do that. The nice thing is that it’s already built in. There are no packages to install, you just enable it my setting isearch-allow-motion to t.


You can start the search at any of:


The current point position
The first match in the file
The last match in the file
The first match before the window
The first match after the window

At the end of each month, I would turn this list into invoices for my different clients. And since every client had their own specific template and invoicing requirements, I didn't bother to set up an automated workflow in Emacs. I just had this list and a little macro that converted it into CSV and I handled the rest manually. (Maybe today, with the power of LLMs, I would try to vibe-code some automation.)



Now, to prepare an invoice, I only needed the lines for that particular client. I did know about the wonderful function flush-lines. It just removes lines matching a regexp. I was already wondering how to negate my regexp used for flush-lines … then I thought: "Maybe there's a sibling function for this purpose?" And behold, Emacs had me covered: M-x keep-lines exists and does exactly what I wanted.



This might sound too small to bother mentioning. And maybe my workflow makes you cringe. But that's that two things that I love about Emacs: You can do things your very own way. And sometimes, improving your workflow doesn't take a package or a custom function. Just finding the command that's already there.



And that is so satisfying about living in Emacs!

Saul “Canelo” Alvarez won another title over the weekend while making a ton of money and looking damn good in the ring. So why is it so easy to feel sorry for him? 
The deserving Mexican legend got past a quick start from reigning WBC super middleweight champion Christian Mbilli, then pounded the essentially unknown underdog champ’s will to win out of him and took his belt via unanimous decision on Saturday in front of a disinterested crowd in a small arena in Riyadh. In the third round, when Canelo had his back against the ropes, he began pounding his own chest and inviting Mbilli to take more shots at him. It's silly to pretend that some otherworldly deity is determining the fates of your favorite sports teams, but what else am I supposed to believe when Lamar Jackson, who had been sidelined with a vaguely described ankle sprain for three games, finally makes it back on the field against the Buffalo Bills on Sunday, only to immediately jam his thumb and leave after one play on offense? The Baltimore Ravens quarterback is most likely out for the rest of the season, as the injury to his throwing hand will require surgery and a trip to the IR.
Watching Jackson leave the game, which the Ravens lost 36-10 after also losing backup QB Tyler Huntley to injury, felt similar to when Aaron Rodgers, fresh from carrying the American flag onto the field as a New York Jet for the first time, was taken out for the season on his first drive. That moment marked the beginning of the end for Rodgers and the Jets, as they never captured the magic they hoped to create (Rodgers went 5-12 as the starter the following season). Will it be the same for Lamar Jackson?
I've been a fan of Jackson since 2016, when I watched him completely dismantle my school, Florida State, while he was at Louisville on his way to winning the Heisman. He's been one of the most exciting players in football for the past decade. Today, though, I can't help but return to the feeling I had in January 2025, when I watched Mark Andrews drop a pass for a two-point conversion in the divisional round of the playoffs against the Bills, a play which could've sent the game to overtime. In that moment, I felt in my bones that it was over for this version of the Ravens. Not necessarily for Jackson, who was playing his best ball at that point, but for the rest of the team.

Elisabetta Palagi, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Pisa, had sent her team of research students to Ethiopia to study geladas, monkeys whose hearts appear to gleam out of their chests. But as her students watched the geladas munch on a grassy plateau alongside other grazing animals, they noticed a peculiar interaction between two other animals. A bull approached a male donkey and mounted him. This behavior did not seem to bother the donkey. The donkey did not kick him or otherwise try to escape the interaction. The researchers contacted Palagi and asked if she thought this cross-species intercourse was worth studying. "I said yes," Palagi wrote in an email.
After close observation, the researchers found that the the bull, dubbed Achille, and the donkey, dubbed Patroclo, have a persistent, mutual sexual relationship, which is described in a new paper in Current Biology. Achille and Patroclo's relationship was not news to the local herders, who laughed when they saw the researchers filming the unexpected pair. "What was an unexpected observation for us was evidently a familiar sight to them," Palagi said. (The paper includes explicit footage of the pair's mating that we have omitted out of respect for their privacy.)
The plateau, with scattered gelada monkeys and Achille and Patroclo nuzzling on the left.

There are two recurring trans women named Carolina in Sloane Murphy's short story collection, Shut Up, I Love You, I'll Call You Tomorrow. One's nicknamed North, and the other's nicknamed South, but nobody can seem to keep track of which is which. "Most of the time she just responds when people call her South," one of the stories says about North, who's the elder of the two. "At least no one was calling her Old Carolina."
This is just one of the details in Murphy's debut that reminded me of the best Hold Steady albums, where casts of lushly described, hard-partying outsiders self-destruct during nights that feel as exciting as they are dangerous. The big difference is that the women in Murphy's stories are trans, which means their stakes are even higher.
Edited by Emily Zhou, who wrote 2023's essential short story collection Girlfriends, Murphy's Shut Up, I Love You does for Trans Chicago what Zhou did for Ann Arbor and Brooklyn. This book announces a talented young writer who crafts stories with a vivid sense of time and place, filled with recognizable conversations and sly humor, punctuated by a willingness to stare at the abyss. But while being trans in 2023 was no great shakes, Murphy's collection arrives at a time when the alarm bells ring even louder—when we can't even watch sports on TV without seeing political ads from one state or another trying to demonize us, trying to tell people we don't deserve to live as we are.
